newsitem.title: UK: Electric retailers pressured by possible MMC move.
newsitem.headline: Electric retailers pressured by possible MMC move.

text.p: Manufacturers and electrical appliances retailers in Britain could face tougher competition as the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) seems set to ban recommended retail prices (RRP).
"It was inevitable that some sort of action had to be taken," Richard Hyman, analyst at Verdict Research, said, referring to a draft MMC report leaked to The Economist magazine.
The Economist reported on Friday that the MMC planned to ban recommended retail prices (RRPs) and to require the manufacturers to promise not to try to control prices.
The MMC, which would not comment on Friday, said the report would be published within six to eight weeks.
Verdict's own research on retail prices of electrical goods conducted earlier this year found that suppliers did call the tune in the electrical retail market which could work against the consumer.
Verdict found that while retailers did not effectively operate a cartel, there was virtual price uniformity.
The manufacturers rejected the allegations.
"We were very concerned at the approach taken by the commission," the Economist quoted Malcolm Wellings of Sony's British arm, as saying.
"It is unusual in a market that suppliers have such a big word on prices," Verdict's Hyman said.
But Britain's leading electrical chain Dixons Group plc, which has about 850 outlets, said on Friday any steps to abolish RRPs would not affect its business.

"As we have explained to the MMC, Dixons does not use RRPs either in its stores or its advertising. Any potential abolition of RRPs is therefore not relevant to our business," Dixons said in the statement.
But the possible ban took its toll as Dixons' shares, which fell 11 pence to 464 pence a share, reflecting the market's view that any step by the MMC could affect the company.
Kingfisher Plc , owner of rival electrical chain Comet which is number two in the market, was down 7p to 713p, but had dropped as low as 705p.
"A wave of discounts could follow and sales could come down", one trader said.
But some analysts had a different view, saying they do not expect a "price war" but that some other big players could enter the market.
"A ban of RRP's would make difficult for independent retailers as they would be squeezed out of the market," Victoria Mendez at Morgan Stanley said.

But the big players would react if Argos Plc, which sells small electrical appliances, televisions and audio, began to offer discounts or moved into selling "white goods" such as washing machines or refrigerators, analysts said.
The Consumers Association has been urging discounts for shoppers.

"We look forward to consumers finally getting a better deal from changes that will also be in the long term interests of the industry," Philip Cullum, head of Policy Research for Consumers' Association, said.
"We are delighted that the MMC appears to be acting to stop the massive collusion between manufacturers and electrical retailers," he added.
Independent research has revealed considerable evidence of price fixing in the industry which would stifle innovation and kept prices high, the Association said.
But the key question remained how to implement the ban, Hyman said, adding that manufacturers could discriminate discount retailers.
"This would be very difficult to prove," Hyman said.
